facts.claim: "This Is the End" is the closing track (track 11) on The Ghost of Paul Revere's album Believe, which was released January 14, 2014.
Believe was recorded live, and produced and mixed by Jonathan Wyman at his studio, The Halo. Adam Ayan mastered it at Gateway.
Discogs credits the band with writing and arranging the album. It lists Max Davis on banjo and vocals and Sean McCarthy on bass and vocals.
The Press Herald lists the Believe lineup as Griffin Sherry (guitar, vocals, octave mandolin), Max Davis (banjo, vocals), Sean McCarthy (bass, vocals) and Matt Young (harmonica).
The Americana Vibes shop lists Believe as a CD with (C) and (P) credited to Americana Vibes.
A 10th-anniversary vinyl edition of Believe came out in 2024 on Americana Vibes. It adds an unreleased track called "Twist" after "This Is the End".
The band formed in 2011 in Portland, Maine. Griffin Sherry (guitar, vocals), Max Davis (banjo, vocals) and Sean McCarthy (bass, vocals) were the original trio.
Believe was the band's first full-length album. It followed the self-released 2012 EP North. "After Many Miles" and "San Antone" each passed two million streams.

Apple Music's biography describes the band as a Portland, Maine Americana group rooted in folk with the energy of rock & roll. It says their later 2017 album Monarch brought greater critical and commercial success.

research.lineage: The band is a Portland, Maine group working in acoustic-driven Americana that is rooted in the folk tradition and has the energy of rock & roll.

draft:
"Give me my last cigarette" is a condemned person's request, and on **This Is the End** The Ghost of Paul Revere make it a chorus a whole room could sing. The song belongs to someone at the very end, someone who dug the grave and figures they might as well get in, yet it moves like a front-porch singalong. Acoustic guitar strums steadily, a banjo runs a bright melodic line over the top, and bass and a simple drum beat hold a relaxed, unhurried pace. The song lives in the gap between what it says and how it sounds.

Watch how the chorus changes. Each time it comes around, the narrator sends a different message home. The mother is told not to worry. The father is told it was worth it. The sister is told not to wait. The last one goes to the friends: tell them I love them. It's a goodbye in installments, the way you'd go around a room, and each errand shows someone trying to shape how they'll be remembered. The message to the father stings most. It could be pride, or a plea for absolution, sent to someone who isn't there to answer.

The verses are where the composure cracks. "I've always hated all the skin I was in" is the confession under the bravado, a lifetime of discomfort set down plainly between invitations to pour a glass and talk about old times. The third verse gets darker and funnier at once, with a gift card for getting cancer and an unanswered question about whether everyone is truly alone. Then comes the line that undoes the cheer: "Just don't ask me if I'm doin' okay," followed by the admission in parentheses that they're not. The narrator wants company but not concern, the drink but not the pity. Those wants sit side by side, and the song never picks one.

The vocal is clear with a little rasp, earnest rather than theatrical. When harmony voices join, the solitary goodbye briefly sounds like a crowd. That fits how it was made. The band formed in Portland, Maine, in 2011 as a trio of guitar, banjo and bass, and they recorded Believe live with Jonathan Wyman producing at his studio, The Halo. The room sounds warm and natural, more gathering than performance. This is Americana built on folk with rock & roll's push, and the song closes the band's first full-length album, a last word that takes its own title literally.

It lets you raise a glass with someone who isn't okay and mean both the toast and the worry, and that is why the chorus keeps coming back to you.
